articles.title: Evidence of a Russian 'hybrid war' in Europe is vanishingly thin - Responsible Statecraft
articles.summary: Evidence of a Russian 'hybrid war' in Europe is vanishingly thin  Responsible Statecraft
articles.full_text:
These days, barely a week goes by in Europe without a drone sighting, a fire or a power outage being blamed on Russia. We’re told that these incidents are all part of a relentless, and escalating, “hybrid war” that Moscow is waging against the continent.
Tensions escalated dramatically last month after Germany formally attributed to Moscow a “failed” drone attack on Leipzig/Halle airport. But does the evidence support Western claims that Russia is engaged in a systematic hybrid war against Europe?
Various datasets and reports are regularly cited as evidence, including from Leiden University, the Soufan Center, the Associated Press and defense-related think tanks like the IISS, CSIS and GLOBSEC. Taken individually, each paints a bleak picture. Read side by side, however, they tell a very different story. For starters, the numbers don’t add up: depending on the report, Russia has launched between 52 and 255 hybrid attacks in Europe since February 2022, a fivefold discrepancy for what is supposed to be the same campaign.
The reason is that there is no agreed-upon definition of what a hybrid attack even is. The IISS itself admits that the term is “amorphous.” Some reports only count acts of physical sabotage; others include pro-Kremlin stickers, graffiti, peace demonstrations and even the Russian Navy passing through the English Channel. In other words, it is a concept that can be used to include almost anything. Moreover, in most cases, the evidence linking Russia is very weak or, in fact, non-existent. Evidence of Russian responsibility usually consists of news articles reporting that Western officials suspect so. If a government claims “Russia did it,” the case ends up on the list.
Yet many of the most widely publicized cases of alleged Russian sabotage — the “jamming” of the GPS signal of von der Leyen’s plane, the Baltic cable incidents in late 2024, a crashed DHL cargo plane, a fire at Heathrow Airport in 2025 — ended up collapsing upon basic scrutiny. In each case, Russian involvement was ultimately ruled out. The signal of von der Leyen’s plane, it turned out, was never lost. The Baltic cables were damaged by anchors dragged by Chinese- and Hong Kong-flagged ships, with investigators finding no evidence of intent. The DHL crash in Vilnius was caused by pilot error, and the Heathrow fire by a fault in a substation that had been identified years earlier but never fixed.But how many people actually know this, considering that such retractions generally receive a fraction of the coverage of the original allegations?
The same goes for the drone panic that swept Europe in the fall of 2025, when near-daily sightings caused the closure of several airports across the continent. Leaders openly blamed Moscow, yet virtually all the “Russian drone” sightings turned out to be unfounded: a Dutch investigation of some 60 incidents found “much panic and hardly any evidence of Russian involvement,” with many sightings turning out to be hobby drones, planes, helicopters, satellites or even stars.
Where Russian drones have indeed entered NATO airspace — in Poland, Romania, Moldova and Lithuania — this has almost always occurred near the Ukrainian border, during attacks on Ukrainian targets. Even the Lithuanian president has stated that the latest such incident was likely caused by a drone that veered off course because of Ukrainian jamming. This appears much more like fallout from the war next door than a deliberate campaign of incursions. There was one incident where a Russian drone was shot down deep in Polish territory, but even in this case Western intelligence officials “privately” admitted that the Russian incursion was probably not intentional.
And then there’s the Leipzig/Halle case. Following Germany’s official accusation of Russian involvement, NATO’s Secretary General Mark Rutte was quick to declare that “the evidence is clear.” This may very well be true, but since no evidence has actually been made public, we simply have to take the German authorities’ word for it. As a German professor told EUobserver, the attribution “may be plausible, but there is evidently no proof.”
Ultimately, once all the speculative and unproven “incidents” are set aside, what remains are a handful of demonstrable sabotage cases that have led to convictions, from a warehouse arson in London to torched buses in Prague,an IKEA fire in Vilnius and some GPS-tracker parcels sent toward Ukraine, allegedly to scout targets and transport routes for sabotage. Even in these cases, however, the courts have convicted low-level recruits, often contacted by anonymous handles on Telegram, and a connection to the Russian state or its proxies was established at a contested trial in only a handful of cases — notably the London warehouse fire and the GPS-tracker parcels in Germany — while elsewhere it rested on guilty pleas or closed hearings. But even assuming that Russia is indeed behind all these cases, the picture that emerges is one of few sporadic incidents with limited damage — hardly the “war” that European leaders routinely invoke.
Subscribe now to our weekly round-up and don't miss a beat with your favorite RS contributors and reporters, as well as staff analysis, opinion, and news promoting a positive, non-partisan vision of U.S. foreign policy.
So is this just a case of collective panic fuelled by click-addicted media? Or, given that the claims of a Russian “hybrid war” against Europe appear to rest on little more than propaganda, is there a concerted effort by the European Union-NATO establishment to condition citizens to believe that Europe is under attack from Russia?
The narrative clearly serves a variety of interests. For starters, it helps governments maintain support for an increasingly unpopular war in Ukraine and for a continental rearmament campaign that will require painful cuts to spending on other sectors. As a report by the Latvian Institute of International Affairs put it, the “nebulous tagline” of hybrid warfare would appear to be driven “by the need to goose flagging defense budgets and waning NATO cohesion.” It has worked: the drone panic has led to increased counter-drone spending at both the EU and NATO levels. Meanwhile, intelligence services have invoked the threat of sabotage to gain broader powers.
The specter of “Russian interference” also offers a broader authoritarian dividend, justifying everything from online censorship to the repression of dissent to election management — most egregiously in Romania, where an entire election was annulled because of an alleged Russian disinformation campaign for which no evidence of Russian involvement was ever provided. More recently, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, amid a push for greater EU ties, said it was “clear” that Russia interfered in the Brexit referendum, without providing any evidence, even though several investigations have found little or no evidence to support this claim.
One may conclude that, to the extent that a “hybrid war” is being waged against Europe, it is being waged by the EU-NATO establishment itself against its own population, in the form of a prolonged campaign of psychological warfare aimed at inflating the Russian threat.
What is most concerning is the risk that this becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. NATO countries continue to enable — through intelligence, satellite and targeting support — Ukrainian deep strikes on Russia, including on civilian infrastructure, and each attack makes Russian retaliation against NATO territory more likely. If and when such an attack comes, it would be framed as an unprovoked escalation of Russia’s ongoing “hybrid war,” leaving little room for European restraint.
This is a classic security dilemma. In such a climate, it would take very little for a “hybrid war” that so far largely exists only on paper to rapidly evolve into a hot war between nuclear-armed powers.
In Italy, the expression “strategy of tension” evokes a dark period, from the late 60s to the early 80s, in which intelligence services and secret paramilitary networks operating under NATO auspices inflated the terrorist threat to frighten the electorate, including by engaging in terrorist acts that in some cases were then blamed on the left. European leaders should be wary of reviving such a strategy.
This article draws on an in-depth investigation published on the author’s Substack.

articles.title: How Russia Sees the World Now
articles.summary: Dmitry Adamsky, an expert on Russian security and Russian nuclear deterrence strategy at Harvard and Reichman Universities, examines a large-scale shift in Russia’s strategic thinking over the past year, centered around the view that Europe, rather than the United States, is now Russia’s primary geopolitical rival and adversary, and looking at the consequences of this shift for US efforts to end the war in Ukraine.
articles.full_text:
In 2022, when Russia launched its full-scale war in Ukraine, the Kremlin’s strategic thinking was shaped around several core ideas. It viewed the United States as its principal geopolitical rival, an adversary that had encouraged Kyiv to impose strategic defeat on Moscow. It considered Europe and NATO largely as an extension of American power. And it saw nuclear muscle flexing as efficient means to exert coercive pressure.
Today, after nearly five years of war, and 22 months of the second Trump administration, the mental map guiding Russian strategy has changed. First, Russia now sees Europe, instead of the United States, as its principal geopolitical adversary, a shift that has driven Russia’s defense establishment to call for an approach known as “castling” to deal with the main threats. Related to this, Moscow now attributes new strategic agency to Europe itself because of the dramatic military modernization taking place in many European countries and the growing interest among some European leaders in developing or extending their own nuclear deterrent. A third shift concerns Russia’s theory of deterrence: Moscow’s traditional understanding of nuclear coercion is giving way to new thinking about nonnuclear strategic deterrence using advanced conventional weapons systems aimed at Europe.
These new lines of thought, which have gained prominence among influential defense intellectuals and policy experts close to the Kremlin over the past year do not need to be endorsed in formal security doctrine to matter. As the past decade has shown, ideas circulating within Russia’s national security establishment have shaped how officials frame problems, define options, and ultimately make major strategic choices. The three recent shifts in Russian strategic thinking will likely play an important part in how Moscow approaches any negotiation to end the war, as well as how it manages future escalation and competition with Europe and the United States.
As the Trump administration steps up its efforts to engage Moscow, it is now negotiating with a Russian leadership whose strategic mindset has evolved considerably since 2022. For the United States, understanding Russia’s new mental map will not only be crucial to any attempt to find an off-ramp with Moscow. It will also be essential to reducing the risk of inadvertent escalation between Russia and Europe and to ensuring strategic stability on the continent in the years to come.
The Pivot To Europe
One of the most notable trends in Russian strategic thought over the past year has been the emergence of the idea of “castling.” A term borrowed from chess, castling in geopolitics describes the repositioning of forces and resources to optimize a state’s strategic posture. Moscow’s defense experts have used the concept to describe a strategy for dealing with a new reality: for the first time since World War II, they have argued, Europe, rather than the United States, has become Russia’s principal geopolitical adversary. According to this view, European countries are now the principal source of Ukraine’s military capacity, political resolve, and strategic resilience; it is Europe and not the United States that has made Ukraine its proxy and is encouraging Kyiv to pursue Moscow’s strategic defeat.
As a consequence, Moscow must direct coercive pressure at Europe—its elites, its decision-making centers, and its critical infrastructure. By doing so, Russia can instill into Europe’s calculus what theorists in Moscow call a “deterring fear”: a European reluctance to antagonize Russia through further support to Ukraine. Such action, they argue, can also rebuild Russian credible deterrence for long-term competition with the West, which is now centered on Europe.
Castling does not imply a change in Russia’s overall objectives, which remain the same as those invoked by Russian President Vladimir Putin at the time of the 2022 invasion. These include banning NATO enlargement to Ukraine and other former Soviet republics; rolling back NATO’s eastern flank; and restricting NATO military exercises, as well as the conventional and nuclear deployments of NATO members, near Russian borders. The difference is that Russian coercion must now be aimed at Europe rather than the United States to achieve these objectives.
Along with this revised assessment of Europe, Russian strategists have interpreted the Trump administration’s own strategic stance as evidence that Asia has replaced Europe as the principal theater of U.S. strategic competition. They point to the administration’s reluctance to back Ukraine, its desire to terminate the war, and its continued overtures to the Kremlin. The administration’s decision in mid-October to provide sanctions relief to Russia and apply new pressure on Ukraine amplify this view in Moscow. Russian strategists also assume Washington seeks to solidify its control of the Western Hemisphere and views China, not Russia, as its primary long-term adversary.
Moscow believes that Washington is thus seeking to reduce its commitments in secondary theaters—particularly Europe and the Middle East—in order to concentrate political, military, and organizational resources on Beijing. As Russia sees it, the new American assertiveness in Venezuela, Cuba, and the Caribbean is unsurprising. By contrast, the current war in Iran—the biggest U.S. military engagement in recent years—has been read in Moscow as an unintended deviation from the new direction of U.S. policy, one that Washington seeks to correct as soon as possible. Whether this reading reflects actual American intentions matters less than that it has become a prevailing understanding in Moscow.
NUCLEAR CURIOSITY
A related trend in Russian discourse is a growing fixation on what defense experts refer to as Europe’s “nuclear curiosity” and new military assertiveness near Russian borders. Specifically, Russian strategists have been concerned by the French and British governments’ modernization of their nuclear programs and apparent readiness to wield them more assertively. Moscow has also noted the prospect of French or British nuclear guarantees extending to European states and nonnuclear European capitals considering the development of nuclear options of their own.
Russian sources identify Germany, Poland, and the Nordic-Baltic states as “nuclear curious,” whether in pursuing nuclear-threshold status or seeking protection under French and British nuclear umbrellas. In this regard, comments by Polish officials in early 2026 expressing support for a Polish nuclear deterrent have been particularly noted. Russian strategists have also closely monitored discussions by Paris and London about offering extended deterrence to the continent as an alternative to the U.S. umbrella.
From Moscow’s perspective, any new attempt by a European state to become a nuclear power would cross a redline and could potentially create a casus belli. Moreover, Europe’s growing assertiveness on nuclear issues is happening in parallel with the deployment of conventional deep-strike precision weapons near Russian borders. For NATO, this more active European posture mitigates the risk of Washington shifting away from its European allies, but to Moscow it signals that Europe could potentially undertake strikes aimed at disarming Russia’s nuclear arsenal or decapitating its leadership.
To Russian analysts, these various developments also suggest Europe’s growing strategic autonomy from the United States. Traditionally, Moscow has viewed Europe largely as a “parking lot” for U.S. forces: a region of the world that is relevant but strategically subordinate to Washington. That assumption is changing. Along with the perception that Europe is now Russia’s principal geopolitical adversary, the continent’s increasing strategic autonomy, including on both nuclear and conventional issues, has become a crucial variable in Russia’s calculus. According to Moscow’s defense intellectuals, Russia may need to change its posture to contain this trend, including by seeking new tools to keep Europe at bay and to coerce it below the nuclear threshold.
MENACING GESTURES
To align with Russia’s new mental map, Russian defense intellectuals and military officers have been examining how to make Moscow’s coercive threats more effective. During the first years of the war, Russia’s nuclear muscle flexing and hybrid warfare failed to prevent Ukraine’s allies from funneling financial support, military aid, and targeting intelligence to Kyiv. This approach also failed to deter Ukraine’s land incursions into Russia and strikes on symbolic Russian targets and Russian strategic infrastructure, let alone compel Kyiv to surrender.
Today, NATO is preoccupied with Russia’s escalating cross-domain coercion, or what U.S. and European analysts call hybrid warfare. But that is only one part of the Russian approach. As Moscow concentrates on Europe as the new primary threat, it is also drawing on new tools of coercion that Russian experts call nonnuclear strategic deterrence. For Russian military authors, NNSD involves using advanced conventional capabilities, including precision-guided weapons, drones, ballistic, cruise, and hypersonic missile systems, as well as “weapons based on new physical principles”—a Russian catchall term for electromagnetic-pulse and high-power microwave weapons to deter and compel adversaries.
Conceptually, NNSD belongs to what Russian experts refer to as the “art of strategic gestures,” a euphemism for using, or threatening to use, nuclear and nonnuclear capabilities to deter and coerce an adversary. Cairo - Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi has asked the country's Parliament to authorize the military to help defend Saudi Arabia after Yemen's intensified their attacks on the kingdom, targeting and oil infrastructure.
Al-Sisi stressed that it would be a defensive mission and only if the kingdom requests assistance.
"Egypt will take any measures requested by Saudi Arabia to protect and defend it," al-Sisi said Saturday during a military graduation ceremony.
Under Egypt's Constitution, the president must consult the National Defense Council and obtain approval from two-thirds of Parliament before deploying the armed forces on a combat mission abroad.
On Sunday, al-Sisi chaired a meeting of the National Defense Council, which reviewed what the Egyptian presidency described as the "grave escalations unfolding in the region" and the "unacceptable attacks" against Saudi Arabia.
The council pledged to provide "all necessary and possible forms of support to the sisterly Kingdom of Saudi Arabia to defend its security and stability, and to safeguard its resources, territorial integrity, and Islamic holy sites."
Egypt has managed, so far, to stay out of all the recent military conflicts in the region and has tried to de-escalate and find political solutions. For some, this is one of al-Sisi's greatest achievements.
But Samir Ragheb, a retired army brigadier and political and strategic analyst, told CBS News that it was time for Egypt to make good on commitments it had made to helping secure the region.
"Egypt has repeatedly pledged to support the security of the Gulf states and has issued numerous statements reaffirming this commitment," Ragheb said. "However, this is a time of war, not politics and statements. If Egypt fails to deliver on these promises, they will lose their meaning and amount to nothing more than empty threats."
"The Gulf states have invested billions of dollars in Egypt. Morally, it's Egypt's turn to return the favor," he said.
Parliament convened an emergency session on Sunday and was expected to approve the resolution on Tuesday, but the vote was postponed until next Monday.
The Egyptian Social Democratic Party instructed its parliamentary bloc to abstain from voting on the resolution, saying in a statement it had not received sufficient information about "the mission's scope, costs, and risks, as well as the arrangements in place to protect Egyptian forces."
Ragheb is certain the region is heading toward a more severe escalation.
"Egypt is not going to defend the kingdom against the Houthis," he said. "The threat is much bigger than the Houthis. This includes Iran, Iraqi militias and sleeper cells within the kingdom itself."
However, he also believes Egypt will lose much of its influence in the region if it doesn't intervene.
"If you want to be a regional player, you must play a role," he said. "Otherwise, you will lose your seat at the table."
Ragheb argued that the United States' in support of Saudi Arabia created a vacuum that must be filled by others. He said Egypt should take on the Arab share of that role.
Other regional powers are also trying to fill the vacuum. In August, Saudi Arabia signed a joint defense agreement with Turkey and Pakistan known as the Mecca Accords.
"Even before Saudi Arabia asked for Egyptian support, the Mecca Accords was a death certificate for the idea of relying on America for any form of defense," Ragheb said.

A weekend of rioting and violence in Milan was caused by a “hybrid war” being waged against the West, Italy’s defence minister warned on Tuesday.
Days of unrest in Italy has seen demonstrators clash with police, loot shops and vandalise property after peaceful protests over the cost of living and public services turned violent.
“The events in Milan and elsewhere in Italy are fundamentally different from those seen in other eras,” Guido Crosetto said.
“They are the product of what I call 'hybrid warfare'—a form of conflict being waged against our nations through unconventional tools like TikTok, social media, and YouTube.”
Mr Crosetto did not mention who he believed was behind the “hybrid” attacks but the phrase is frequently used to describe Russian attempts to destabilise Europe through the spread of disinformation and cyberattacks. European officials have recently warned that Moscow is stepping up a hybrid campaign on the continent.
Crosetto argued that the West had been slow to respond to the threat, saying young people may be receiving a ‘counter-education’ outside of school and the family.
Italy was due to approve new security measures on Tuesday targeting minors, politicians said, in response to two days of unrest that saw hooded protesters set bins ablaze and shops looted.
Law enforcers will be allowed to detain people under the age of 18 at police stations for 12 hours, even if they have not committed a crime, provided there is evidence they pose a danger, deputy PM Matteo Salvini said.
Rome is also expected to deploy an additional 500 army troops in Milan as authorities fear more unrest at demonstrations planned for Saturday.
"From words to action: 500 more troops to defend Milan," Mr Salvini, who leads the co-ruling right-wing League party, said in a post on X.
Luxury shops in Milan's Via Montenapoleone shopping district, including Chanel, Tiffany and Dior, have removed expensive merchandise from their windows over fears of another day of rioting.
Sports retailers Decathlon and Arc'teryx and mobile phone operator Vodafone were all ransacked over the weekend, while other brands including Levi’s, Under Armour, and Decathlon all covered their shop windows.
Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni, who is seeking reelection in next year’s general election, condemned the violence, saying: “Thugs who exploit demonstrations to sow chaos, attack those who ensure security, and hold entire cities hostage. Demonstrating is a right. Setting our cities ablaze is not.”
Foreign minister Antonio Tajani, who also serves as deputy prime minister like Salvini, wrote on X: "The government will respond firmly to these attacks on the state, including through measures aimed at curbing violence by minors.”
As part of a planned crackdown on the protests, Meloni is considering extending preventive detention for minors and cracking down on youth gangs, Corriere della Sera newspaper reported, accelerating provisions from an existing security bill currently being scrutinised by parliament.
Italian police said it had detained 271 young people during unrest in Milan on Sunday. Of those taken to police stations, 32 were arrested, including 23 minors and 13 foreign nationals, police said on Monday. A further 28 people were reported to judicial authorities.
The unrest followed clashes on Saturday in Milan and other northern cities including Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo and Turin, where 28 protesters were arrested, according to a police report released on Sunday.
The disturbances echoed unrest in neighbouring France, where hundreds of thousands of people angered by rising living costs and declining public services took to the streets on Saturday in some of the country's most violent protests in years.
A new set of curfews is set to be imposed in France tonight, prime minister Sebastien Lecornu has said, saying the measures last night contributed to “calm” across the country.
“Targeted curfews have contributed to the calm of this night,” Mr Lecornu said, adding that new curfews would be decided “on the ground, by the prefects, in coordination with the mayors”.
Last night, the French government imposed partial curfews across the country, including in Paris and Nice, after riots and looting amid nationwide protests over the weekend.

articles.title: Yemen war turmoil: Crafting a strategic framework - Pakistan Observer
articles.summary: Yemen war turmoil: Crafting a strategic framework  Pakistan Observer
articles.full_text:
THE peace fulcrum of the Middle East—historically balanced on a fragile equilibrium between Gulf stability, global energy transit and proxy deterrence—has been fundamentally shattered by the collapse of the Saudi-Houthis 2022 truce and the renewal of war between them. Driven by the broader geopolitical fallout– of the regional war involving Iran, Israel and the United States, on the one side and the non-state actors, on the other — has rippled outward, destabilizing the entire region.
The Houthi-Saudi conflict has upped the ante as it disrupts the Middle East’s peace fulcrum by escalating regional tensions undermining diplomatic efforts and fueling proxy warfare. This struggle intensifies instability in Yemen, strains Gulf alliances and threatens vital maritime routes like the Red Sea, impacting global trade and security. The conflict also complicates U.S. and international mediation, as competing interests hinder unified solutions. Ultimately, prolonged hostilities weaken state institutions, deepen humanitarian crises and create power vacuums exploited by extremist groups.
In response to devastating Houthi strikes—such as the recent attack on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport that killed 13 people—Saudi Arabia has activated the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement with Turkey and Pakistan. Although Iran recently offered to mediate between the Houthis and Riyadh, Saudi Arabia views the Houthis’ deep strikes as direct extensions of Iranian strategy, rendering bilateral trust obsolete and polarizing the region back into rigid pro- and anti-Iran blocs.
Ironically, what began as a civil war in 2014 has fundamentally transformed into an internationalized node of a larger global confrontation. The US has reassessed its military footprint, weighing direct interventions and strikes against Houthi positions, while Western allies like France and the UK are deploying defensive assets to assist Riyadh. This turns the southern tip of the Arabian Peninsula into a high-stakes proxy arena, where any miscalculation by local actors can drag global superpowers into a direct military confrontation.
For years, the domestic peace of the Gulf cooperated with grand economic transformations—chiefly Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030. The peace fulcrum allowed these nations to transition into hubs for international tourism, multi-billion-dollar sports franchises, entertainment and global tech investments. By launching targeted drone and missile strikes against Saudi Aramco facilities in Jizan and Yanbu, alongside the East-West pipeline, the Houthis have successfully weaponized oil infrastructure. This volatility directly upsets the global energy market and impacts broader economic stability.
This is now a growing truth that the Yemen conflict has intensified regional and global power struggles, transforming the country into a proxy battleground between Saudi Arabia and Iran, with broader implications for US and Chinese strategic interests. This escalation fuels instability across the Middle East, as superpowers leverage alliances, arms sales and diplomatic influence to expand their regional dominance. The war’s humanitarian toll and geopolitical entanglement underscore how local conflicts can become flashpoints in larger great-power competition.
Resolving the ongoing crisis requires shifting away from outdated diplomatic frameworks. With the UN Special Envoy warning that Yemen has fallen back into full-scale war following major military escalations, the international community must transition from reactive management to active, multi-layered structural solutions. 1-Traditional diplomacy has long treated the war strictly as a binary struggle between the Houthis and the internationally recognized government. The International Crisis Group highlights that this approach ignores deep factional fragmentation. Future peace talks must dynamically integrate diverse localized stakeholders, including the Southern Transitional Council (STC), independent civil society and women-led coalitions. 2- Forming a dedicated mediation council consisting of the UN P5 members, the European Union and the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) should be formed. This would create a unified diplomatic ledger to distribute negotiation responsibilities and prevent individual nations from acting as isolated spoilers.
3- Enforcing Maritime Laws in the Red Sea: To protect the global economy and local supply lines, the international community must strictly isolate Yemen from broader Middle Eastern flare-ups. This demands a firm defense of commercial navigation rights, alongside tailored pressure on regional state actors to curb weapons smuggling and funding to local factions.
4- Channelizing high-level western and regional diplomatic overtures with Iran must directly condition broader regional concessions on the material de-escalation of support for Houthi military actions. 5-Depoliticising State Resources: Much of the war is driven by disputes over resources, port fees, public-sector payrolls and the division of the central bank. The international community should condition future state recognition on the implementation of an independent joint economic sharing.
6-Close the Funding Gap: The UN’s humanitarian response plan remains drastically underfunded, leaving roughly two-thirds of the population in dire need of assistance. International donors must explicitly fulfill funding commitments through organizations like the IOM & UNICEF. 7-Spearheading conditional Aid on Worker Safety: In response to arbitrary Houthi detentions of aid personnel, international actors must universally apply strict diplomatic pressure, conditioning non-lifesaving assistance on the unhindered access and absolute safety of humanitarian workers.
While tensions persist, major powers have shown restraint in avoiding direct military escalation. International institutions, arms control agreements and economic interdependence act as stabilizing forces. The Forum of 4—comprising Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Turkey and Egypt—has engaged in diplomatic efforts to support a political resolution to the Yemen crisis. These nations have advocated for inclusive negotiations, humanitarian access and a ceasefire, leveraging their regional influence to encourage dialogue between the warring parties, including the Houthi movement and the internationally recognized Yemeni government. History shows that crises often escalate rhetorically but de-escalate through negotiation. Current efforts by regional actors and mediators must reflect this pattern.
—The writer is an independent IR & International Law analyst.

articles.title: Putin and Zelenskyy back three-way US peace talks on Ukraine - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: Putin and Zelenskyy back three-way US peace talks on Ukraine  Al JazeeraMissiles hit Kyiv after Russia agrees to US call to resume Ukraine peace talks  BBCUkraine war briefing: New peace proposals lack ‘substance’, says Kremlin after Witkoff-Putin meeting in Russia  The GuardianWitkoff salutes ‘humanitarian’ Putin  The TelegraphPutin agrees to resume 3-way peace talks with Ukraine and US  Reuters
articles.full_text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy have both expressed support for a United States proposal to hold three-way talks to end the conflict in Ukraine.
The Kremlin said Putin conveyed his “in principle” willingness to engage in negotiations during a meeting in St Petersburg with US special envoy Steve Witkoff on Wednesday.
Speaking to journalists via WhatsApp as he returned to Kyiv from Norway, Zelenskyy confirmed Ukraine’s interest in the talks, which he said should take place no later than early November.
Zelenskyy added that he had spoken with US officials following Witkoff’s discussions with Putin.
“We have received feedback that… Russia supports a trilateral meeting at the level of our [negotiating] teams,” Zelenskyy said.
“The American side has proposed holding it as soon as possible and we support that… The Ukrainian side has been in contact with its American partners. They will do everything to ensure that the meeting takes place as early as possible, in November. I think no later than early November.”
Zelenskyy said Kyiv supports “any proposals for a ceasefire, an end to the war, an energy ceasefire as well as humanitarian initiatives”.
The diplomatic effort comes as Washington pushes for an end to the war in Ukraine, which began more than four and a half years ago with Moscow’s full-scale invasion.
Witkoff held talks with Putin on Wednesday after meeting with Ukrainian and European officials in Norway a day earlier.
“Steve Witkoff briefed Vladimir Putin on the substance of the talks held in Oslo,” Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters, referring to talks Witkoff held in Norway with Ukrainian and European officials on Tuesday.
“He mentioned some new aspects in the approaches of the Europeans and Kyiv … but there wasn’t really much substance in them.”
“Our president informed Steve Witkoff that we are, in principle, ready to resume the mentioned talks [with Washington and Kyiv],” he added, saying they could take place in mid-November.
He later told Russian state television Vesti that the talks may be held in Abu Dhabi.
The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February before the United States and Israel launched a war against Iran.
Goodwill gesture
The three-hour talks in a grand imperial palace in St Petersburg, the ninth time that Witkoff has met Putin in person, began with a goodwill gesture from Russia – the release of Stephen Hubbard, a retired US teacher held in Russia.
Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova, reporting from Moscow, said Russia is obviously interested in the lifting of international sanctions, and US sanctions in particular.
“The Trump administration is using economic leverage to encourage Moscow to finish this war, including the temporary lifting of US sanctions on Russian diesel sales,” she said.
Putin also thanked US President Donald Trump and Witkoff for their efforts to end the war.
Ukraine and Russia remain far apart when it comes to the terms of any possible peace deal, but Trump has recently intensified pressure on Ukraine to “make a deal”. He said on Tuesday that it was time for Ukraine to end the war or face “a very bad thing”.
Putin also offered to help Trump in dealing with Iran, saying Moscow had a decades-long relationship with Tehran, which it has repeatedly offered to leverage to address US concerns about Iran’s nuclear programme.
Russia could also supply large quantities of fertiliser to the US to help farmers, Putin told Witkoff.
A potential meeting in China next month with Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping was also discussed. The Kremlin said Beijing was already preparing what it said would be the first trilateral meeting of its kind in history.
Oslo talks
The talks in Russia come a day after Witkoff met Ukraine’s Zelenskyy and European leaders in Norway. Witkoff briefed Putin on the Oslo talks, which he described as productive and said had been characterised by “some degree of momentum”.
The prime ministers of Norway and Finland also attended the talks in Oslo. Representatives from the European Union and NATO were present. Following Tuesday’s talks, Zelenskyy said that “very, very important” intelligence from the US had been restored.
US-Ukraine ties have deteriorated sharply since Trump announced a diesel export deal with Russia earlier this month.
Zelenskyy has also accused Washington of slowing down the internet service Starshield, which is crucial for Ukraine’s battlefield operations. Starshield is the military-grade equivalent of Starlink – both developed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX.
As diplomatic efforts intensify, Russia and Ukraine continue to trade long-range attacks.
At least one person was killed and two were wounded in a Ukrainian drone attack in Russia’s western Bryansk region on Wednesday, Governor Yegor Kovalchuk said on Telegram.
The Ukrainian emergency service said two people were killed in a Russian attack on a high-rise building in the Sviatoshynskyi district of the capital, Kyiv.

Russia’s Presidential Administration has ordered state and Kremlin-aligned media outlets to begin writing about “Putin strikes” on Ukraine, two employees at such outlets told Meduza.
The Presidential Administration’s political bloc sent loyalist media recommendations advising them to report that “the effectiveness and efficiency of Russia’s strikes far exceed what the Ukrainian military has achieved.”
“Our ballistic weapons have performed flawlessly. The Ukrainian regime has lost its most important production and storage sites, where cruise missiles and drones, along with their components, were assembled and stored. ‘Putin strikes’ are far larger in scale and more effective than enemy attacks. We are shutting down the militants’ missile programs, which helps keep Russia’s regions secure,” the guidance document says.
Headlines, comments from servicemen, and articles using the phrase “Putin strikes” indeed appeared this week in major Russian media outlets.
For example, the Russian news website Gazeta.ru published an article with the following subheadline:
“SVO” veteran Konovalov: “Putin strikes” deprive the Ukrainian military of the ability to fight.
The outlet cites Vitaly Konovalov, head of the Association of Veterans of the Russia-Ukraine War in Stavropol Krai, who says the strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure are allegedly aimed at undermining supplies to the Ukrainian military. Notably, Konovalov himself never uses the phrase “Putin strikes.” It appears in the connecting phrases and generalizations added by propagandists.
Novye Izvestia published an article titled “Putin Strikes on Ukraine: Ukrainian Military Left Without Electricity and Weapons.” Rosbalt used the phrase in the headline of a news item titled “Putin Strikes on Ukraine: Ukrainian Military Losing Logistics Hubs, Substations, and Vessels.” It also appears in headlines and articles from Fedpress. Segodnia.ru writes about a “series of “Putin strikes.”” The phrase has even appeared in pro-government Instagram accounts.
A political consultant who works with the Presidential Administration’s political bloc said directly linking Putin to the strikes on Ukraine is meant to try to boost the president’s approval ratings.
According to polls by the Public Opinion Foundation (FOM), Putin’s approval rating fell from 75% in July to 71% in early October, while trust in him fell from 74% to 70% over the same period.
“In this case, [the idea is to raise the ratings] among the pro-war, ultra-patriotic segment of society, who need to be shown some successes from the war. To the question “What has been accomplished?” [at the front], the suggested answer is “Putin strikes,” by analogy with the “Stalinist strikes,”” the consultant said.
During Joseph Stalin’s rule, the term “Ten Stalinist Strikes” referred to 10 major Soviet army operations during World War II.
The source told Meduza that it is hard to assess how effective the appearance of “Putin strikes” in the press has been: “Maybe it will have some effect on the older segment [of society].”
Speaking at a press conference in Bishkek on September 1, following the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit, Vladimir Putin said he had ordered the Russian military to prepare and carry out massive strikes on Ukraine’s energy facilities. “They’re striking our people, so they’ll get a response,” he added.

They took the first step. We started responding. Now they’re whining about energy facilities too, and about other targets, including data centers and so on. They started it. They shouldn’t have started it.

North Korea says it will resume propaganda broadcasts across border into South Korea
SEOUL, South Korea (AP) — North Korea plans to resume anti-Seoul propaganda broadcasts along the heavily armed border with South Korea, leader Kim Jong Un’s sister said, reviving a psychological warfare campaign as tensions rise after land mine blasts injured three South Korean front-line soldiers.
Kim Yo Jong, her brother’s top spokesperson on Washington and Seoul, made the announcement Wednesday after visiting front-line areas where North Korean troops are reinforcing the border. She renewed a threat to retaliate against any South Korean provocation aimed at the fortification work.
In a follow-up statement Thursday, she said the North would place “new counter means” on alert along the border and have its loudspeakers on “standby” within days.
North Korea has been adding mines, barbed wire fences, anti-tank barriers and other fortifications to what’s already one of the world’s most heavily armed borders as Kim Jong Un pushes a hard line toward Seoul.
Touring the area with Marshal Pak Jong Chon, one of her brother’s top military officials, Kim Yo Jong called the fortification work a “sacred and great undertaking” supporting the leader’s policy of permanently severing ties with South Korea, which he has declared his most hostile adversary amid a broader diplomatic stalemate with Washington.
“Our tactical hunting teams are taking new positions, and within October, the loudspeakers for psychological warfare against the ROK will be in operation along the whole border,” Kim Yo Jong said, using the initials of South Korea’s formal name, the Republic of Korea.
She warned that if South Korean warning shots — which Seoul says are meant to force North Korean soldiers doing fortification work back across the border — cause “actual harm to our territorial security and our service persons’ safety,” North Korean border guards “will show no mercy for the armed gangsters bereft of reason.”
Asked about Kim Yo Jong’s threat to resume the loudspeaker broadcasts, South Korean Defense Ministry spokesperson Chung Binna said Thursday that Seoul would need to take “proportionate measures” in response to the North’s moves along the border, but did not elaborate on what steps are being considered.
North Korea’s state-run Korean Central News Agency first reported Kim’s border visit as Tuesday, but Kim later corrected it to early Wednesday in a separate statement.
Following an inspection with the U.S.-led United Nations Command, Seoul formally blamed North Korean-planted mines for the Sept. 21 border blasts and urged the North to apologize and clear its remaining mines. North Korea denied responsibility for the explosions and warned of strong retaliation if provoked.
“Our military leadership underlined the need to make those rogues aware that our new firepower units have taken their firing positions,” Kim told soldiers during her visit Wednesday, reminding them of her brother’s order to make the border with the “enemy ... eternally impregnable.”
South Korea’s military has said North Korean soldiers crossed the border’s military demarcation line 50 times this year during fortification work, and that it responded with warning shots and broadcasts. Kim has said South Korean’s claims of border crossings are a “false pretext,” and that its provocations have increased “beyond the red line” since the mine blasts.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff chairman, Jin Yong-Sung, called Kim’s threats “intolerable” and ordered the military to “sternly respond” to potential provocations by the North.
During Tuesday’s border inspection, Pak accused the South of making “deliberate, premeditated and absurd” claims to shift blame over the rising tensions and threatened an “overwhelming response” to South Korean provocations. He also denied that the North Korean soldiers were breaching the border during fortification work, saying “our army knows where our borderline is better than any others,” KCNA said.
Loudspeaker broadcasts are among the Cold War-era psychological warfare tactics the two Koreas have occasionally used against each other during times of tensions.
South Korea’s liberal government, led by President Lee Jae Myung, halted its broadcasts after taking office last year to improve ties with the North, which later stopped its own.
Kim Jong Un in recent years has cut off all diplomacy and cooperation with South Korea and declared it a permanent enemy as a yearslong stalemate in nuclear negotiations with Washington drags on.

articles.summary: Across the Border: North Koreans Work on the Southern Border Fence  38 NorthNorth Korea's Kim Yo Jong warns South Korea, says border loudspeakers to be ready within days  ReutersNorth Korea tells border troops to take ‘resolute action’ if South threatens their safety  CNNSouth Korea vows resolute punishment over Kim Yo Jong’s weapon threat  The IndependentNorth Korea Says Loudspeakers Will Be Ready Near Border in Days  Bloomberg.com
articles.full_text:
North Korea is currently carrying out an intensive upgrade of its southern border in the Kaesong area, directly across the Han River from South Korea.
During a visit to the area in mid-September, hundreds of workers were visible engaged in manual construction work along the border fence while blasting could be seen in the distance. A reporting team from Japanese broadcaster NHK observed similar scenes when they visited in early October.
The inter-Korean border has always been heavily guarded but in the years since the Covid pandemic, North Korea has sought the strengthen its border regions with stronger and additional fencing. It has also deployed electronic surveillance devices along the border making escape and infiltration increasingly difficult.
The images in this article were captured from South Korea’s Aegibong Peace Ecological Park in Gimpo, Gyeonggi Province. From there, the closest point of the North Korean shoreline is just over 1.7 kilometers away. The workers were photographed approximately 3 kilometers away, and the blastingcaptured was just over 7 kilometers away.
What appears to be two fences on the satellite image are more elaborate arrangements when viewed up close. They would make it difficult for anyone to illicitly cross from either direction.
Someone approaching the border from inside the country would first have to make it through or over the inner fence. This is the simpler of the two and appears designed to keep most people away from the actual border. The distance between it and the outer fence varies along the border and, in some places, agricultural land lies between the two, suggesting some citizens are allowed access through this fence.
The outer fence, closest to the border, is not a single fence but a succession of what appear to be three electrified layers. On the inside, the first layer has about eight electrified wires. There is then a gap around one meter-wide to a central layer that is also electrified and extends higher up. Finally, the third layer has electric wires on the inside of the posts and a wire lattice main fence, topped with barbed wire.
Not all of the border area is so well defended. Some sections still contain older electrified fencing and in other areas, the posts and fences have been installed, but the electrification has not been completed. The work observed appears to be part of the ongoing upgrade to improve these weaker areas.
Over 100 people appeared to be working on the border road, just a little further along from a section where the new fencing was already in place. A few new concrete fencing poles had already been erected in the work zone and workers seemed to be leveling and widening the road.
The workers were a cross section of society: young and old, men and women; they were wearing casual clothes and either shoveling dirt or resting from the physical work. Except for a single truck that was hauling dirt and rocks, no machinery appeared to be in use.
In North Korea, citizens can be pressed into compulsory manual labor as both a punishment or simply to support the state. It is likely this group was comprised of the latter as the state would be sensitive about prisoners being seen from South Korea. They were likely residents of the area forcibly mobilized by the state.
Border guards with rifles over their shoulders were stationed around the worksite. Their presence was likely to deter anyone from hopping over the old fence, because the work was happening right up against it. Had anyone tried, they would still have faced a swim of about a kilometer to reach the South Korean side, so it would not have been easy anyway.
For one of the workers, the day took a bad turn. In two images taken four seconds apart, the worker can be seen with his back towards two soldiers, first with his hands on his head and then behind his back. The sequence was only noticed during a later review of the images, so no other video or photo evidence of what he might have done or how he was handled afterwards exists. The workers around him do not seem to be drawn to the spectacle and are looking down a road, possibly at something approaching.
Further along the border, a little over 7 kilometers from the observation position, blasting was taking place. Three blasts were heard over an hour-long period although their exact purpose was unclear.
Also along the shoreline, a truck was visible dumping dirt and rocks on a rocky beach area.
Upgrades along this stretch of the border have been underway for some time. Many of the guard posts were upgraded with new cameras in 2023. The cameras are equipped with additional sensors, likely infrared or radar, for monitoring movement at nighttime.
Electronic surveillance along the border has also made escape or infiltration more difficult. Along the northern border, North Koreans have historically crossed into China for informal trading often after bribing border guards. There, electronic surveillance has also been deployed.
The cameras in the north serve to both deter illegal crossings but also bribery because they can be used to ensure guards are doing their job and not letting people cross.
The success of the greater border defenses can be seen in data on the number of North Koreans escaping the country. In the first six months of this year, 63 North Koreans arrived in South Korea, down from the 96 who arrived in the same period of 2025.
Numbers have dropped significantly since North Korea began strengthening its borders and many of the arrivals into South Korea are not recent defections but people who left the country years ago and have been living in China or Southeast Asia.

Violent protests have broken out across Europe amid growing frustration over the cost of living crisis, a lack of affordable housing and deteriorating school conditions.
As many as 550,000 people turned out across France on Saturday, according to authorities, to demonstrate against declining public services. Protests turned violent in Paris as shops were looted and cars set on fire in some of the city’s worst violence in years.
Young people waved Italian flags and let off flares in Milan as they rallied against the rising cost of living in scenes that were condemned by prime minister Giorgia Meloni.
Police used water cannon and teargas to break up the crowds after some masked rioters clashed with authorities and set off fires.
Tens of thousands of people meanwhile marched through central Lisbon in protest of the soaring cost of living and a deepening housing crisis, echoing weeks of demonstrations in Spain that prompted prime minister Pedro Sanchez to call a snap general election.
Pressure was also on Albania’s prime minister Edi Rama after a week of protests over poor university conditions, high tuition fees and corruption, which saw hours-long violent clashes with police on Sunday.
Here we look at the factors behind the protests sweeping the continent and the latest developments.
France
Marseille is set to impose a curfew on minors each night until Friday in response to the violent protests that have rocked France.
On Monday night, the French government imposed partial curfews across the country, including in Paris and Nice, after riots and looting amid nationwide protests over the weekend.
It came after thousands of rioters were arrested during the weekend’s widespread protests, with justice minister Gérald Darmanin promising an “unrelenting” response to violence. The unrest gathered momentum from student-led demonstrations that began last month in response to overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages.
Authorities said more than half a million people turned out to march on Saturday, including 110,000 in Paris alone. Organisers put the figure closer to 800,000.
While hundreds of thousands protested peacefully across France on Saturday, violent fringe groups targeted public buildings, looted luxury boutiques and supermarkets, and attacked police vehicles and officers.
French president Emmanuel Macron appealed for calm on Sunday as some of the protests boiled over into violent clashes with police. The government has blamed the violence on what it said were ultra-left groups, as well as criminals it said had instigated the looting.
More than 2,400 people were arrested across France, while nearly 1,000 officers were injured, according to the government. Police fired teargas in Paris on Sunday afternoon and protesters set fire to piles of bicycles.
One protester died on Saturday after suffering a cardiac arrest during demonstrations in the capital.
Spain
Tens of thousands of people have turned out across Spain in recent weeks following the eviction of 87-year-old Maria del Carmen Abascal, known as Maricarmen, from her Madrid home.
The pensioner was forcibly removed from her flat of 70 years after the property was bought by the investment firm Urbagestion, which tried to increase her rent by 230 per cent. She died suddenly in early October, two weeks after she was evicted.
Maricarmen’s death reinvigorated a movement long frustrated by home shortages and surging rents across the country.
Socialist prime minister Pedro Sanchez last month called a snap general election for 29 November after parliament rejected his government’s proposals to address a mounting housing crisis.
Several people who received eviction orders have died by suicide in Spain in recent months.
Spain's minimum wage is €1,221 (£1,025), while the average monthly rent for an 80-square-meter apartment is around €1,130 (about £949), according to an analysis by the business newspaper Expansión.
Italy
“Italia in Piazza,” or Italy in the Streets, has galvanized thousands of demonstrators against crumbling public services and the rising cost of living.
Milan police clashed on Sunday with protesters throwing stones and looting shops. Meanwhile, police in riot gear fired teargas and used water cannons after several hundred hooded protesters broke shop windows and set bins on fire in the area near central Piazza Duomo, sources told Reuters, adding that more than 60 protesters had been detained for checks.
A total of 28 protesters were arrested after similar clashes erupted on Saturday in northern cities including Milan, Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo and Turin, according to a police report on Sunday.
Ms Meloni, facing an election next year, condemned the violence and announced a government meeting on Monday to discuss how to address the situation.
Now a newly formed group calling itself the “17 October Movement” has announced what it describes as a “permanent mobilization” to demonstrate every Saturday at 3 p.m. in cities across Italy.
Portugal
Fifty-five people were arrested as Portuguese police dismantled housing crisis protest camps in the central squares of Lisbon and Porto before dawn on Tuesday.
Activists pitched roughly 200 tents in Lisbon’s Rossio square on Saturday, while Porto’s Dom Joao I square had been occupied for 10 days. Protesters say low wages are failing to keep pace with housing costs and the rising cost of living, leaving many people struggling to make ends meet.
Portugal faces an acute housing affordability crisis, where buying costs have more than doubled since 2017 and new lease rents have almost doubled.
Urban areas feel the greatest strain, compounded by backlash against excessive tourism and digital nomads. Activists want the centre-right government to drop a bill easing evictions and removing rent caps on new leases, which passed its first reading after the far-right Chega party abstained.
Tens of thousands of people also marched through central Lisbon on Saturday. Portugal's biggest union, CGTP, which called the rally, said “many tens of thousands” packed one of the capital's main avenues.
Portugal’s inflation hit 3.6 per cent in September, driven by rising food and fuel prices, the latter up 15 per cent year-on-year following an increase in tensions in the Middle East.
Albania
Anti-government protests have stretched over a week in Albania's capital of Tirana, with clashes escalating after high school and university students joined the broad anti-government “Flamingo” movement calling for Socialist Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.
Rama has condemned the protesters as “ideologized and radicalized” by antifa, an umbrella term for loosely organized far-left militants in the United States, where President Donald Trump has designated the movement a terrorist organization.
Ending corruption is a major demand of the movement, which was named for the natural habitat of flamingos in an area where Rama's government agreed to allow a major luxury tourism development linked to Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law. They also want protections for healthcare, education, and public pensions, according to its website.
Serbia
Tens of thousands of people are expected to march in Serbia’s capital Belgrade on Thursday as part of an election rally led by student activists.
For nearly two years, Serbian university students have driven mass anti-corruption protests. Now they share a broader aim: defeating the nation's powerful populist leader Aleksandar Vucic in this weekend's early parliamentary election.
Following the 25 October vote, the former authoritarian president is seeking a return as prime minister to extend his right-wing party's 14-year rule. Having previously rattled the populists during their demonstrations, Serbia's youth movement is the sole barrier in his way.
Unlike high school students in France who are rallying for better education, Serbia's student movement started out as a struggle for justice after a train station tragedy in the country's north killed 16 people in November 2024. The students' call for accountability for the deaths, which they blamed on rampant corruption, found widespread support. Protests spread, forcing a government collapse and rattling Vucic.
Much is uncertain ahead of Sunday's vote. Tensions remain high alongside the stakes. Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party, or SNS, and the student-supported Students' List are thought to be running close, leaving the outcome uncertain and raising fears of potential violence.

Zelensky Opens Door to Peace Deal Freezing Current Battle Lines
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said he would accept a peace deal freezing the conflict with Russia along current frontlines, marking a significant shift in Kyiv's stance.
Speaking during a Fox News interview on Wednesday, Zelensky addressed ongoing efforts to bring the war to an end while appearing to rebuild ties with President Donald Trump following recent tensions between the two leaders, according to Washington Examiner.
When questioned by host Brian Kilmeade on the program Fox & Friends about whether he would accept a deal freezing territorial control at present battle lines, the Ukrainian president confirmed he would be willing to consider such an arrangement.
Diplomatic Repositioning
The statement represents a notable evolution in Zelensky’s public position on ending the conflict. Throughout much of the war, Ukrainian leadership has maintained that full territorial restoration, including Crimea and the Donbas region, would be necessary for any lasting settlement.
The interview comes at a critical juncture as Trump has repeatedly pledged to bring the Russia-Ukraine war to a swift conclusion, though specific details of any proposed peace framework remain unclear.
Strategic Calculations
Zelensky’s remarks appear calculated to align more closely with the Trump administration’s approach to the conflict, following what Washington Examiner characterized as a recent falling out between the two leaders. Maintaining strong relations with Washington remains essential for Ukraine’s continued military and financial support.
The willingness to discuss a territorial freeze represents a pragmatic acknowledgment of battlefield realities, even as Ukrainian forces continue defensive operations against Russian advances in the eastern regions.

articles.title: China says it is 'safeguarding order' around Taiwan-controlled South China Sea atoll - AsiaOne.com
articles.summary: China says it is 'safeguarding order' around Taiwan-controlled South China Sea atoll  AsiaOne.com
articles.full_text:
BEIJING — China's government said on Wednesday (Oct 20) that its coast guard was "safeguarding order" around a tiny and strategically located Taiwan-controlled atoll at the top end of the South China Sea where Taipei fears Beijing is trying to enforce jurisdiction.
China, which views democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory, said last week that Taiwan must "bear the consequences" of its coast guard using a water cannon against a Chinese fishing boat near the Pratas Islands.
Taiwan has reported two incidents since Sunday of Chinese coast guard vessels approaching the Pratas, accusing Beijing of provocative behaviour.
Speaking at a regular news briefing, a spokesperson for China's Taiwan Affairs Office said Beijing has "indisputable sovereignty" over the South China Sea islands, including the Pratas and their adjacent waters.
"Mainland coast guard vessels conducting law enforcement patrols in the relevant waters are fulfilling their duties in accordance with the law, safeguarding normal navigation and operational order," spokesperson Zhang Han told reporters.
The Chinese ships are "effectively protecting the lawful and legitimate rights and interests of people on both sides of the Taiwan Strait and the safety of lives and property", she added.
The "obstinate insistence" by Taiwan's ruling party on its separatist stance is the root cause of the peril of war across the strait, Zhang said.
Taiwan's government rejects Beijing's territorial claims, saying only the Taiwanese people can decide their future.
China recognises no claims of sovereignty by Taiwan and has never renounced the use of force to bring the island under its control.
The Pratas have no permanent civilian population and lie roughly between southern Taiwan and Hong Kong. Security experts see them as vulnerable to Chinese attack due to their distance — more than 400 km — from Taiwan.
Chinese 'law enforcement'
China's military already operates around Taiwan on an almost daily basis. Taipei has become increasingly alarmed by Beijing's use of its coast guard to carry out "law enforcement" patrols to try to assert jurisdiction.
Addressing a forum in Taipei late Tuesday, Taiwan's top China-policy maker said Beijing is attempting to "domesticate" the Taiwan issue to "create an illusion of having de facto jurisdiction over Taiwan's surrounding waters and offshore islands".
With President Xi Jinping expected to be confirmed for a fourth term in office next year, China's mission to "achieve national unification" becomes even more pressing, said Chiu Chui-cheng, head of the Mainland Affairs Council.
"We assess that Beijing's Taiwan policy will shift toward a more aggressive, provocative strategy of 'exercising jurisdiction before achieving unification'," he added.
Source: Reuters

articles.summary: NATO activates plan to protect the Black Sea.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Speaking after an emergency meeting of the North Atlantic Council held on October 20 in Brussels, Belgium, NATO spokesperson Allison Hart confirmed that the Alliance would immediately deploy additional military assets to the Black Sea, focusing on surveillance, aerial reconnaissance, and field technical analysis.
A NATO representative stated: “NATO will deploy additional resources in the region, including surveillance, reconnaissance, and technical investigation support. We continue to act in solidarity, ready to counter any threat and protect the safety of our citizens.”
The NATO Ambassadorial Meeting was triggered at the urgent request of Romania and Bulgaria, two member states directly affected by recent maritime security developments.
Since the beginning of October, a series of serious incidents have occurred in the Exclusive Economic Zones (EEZs) of Bulgaria and Romania. Numerous cargo ships and oil tankers have been attacked by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) both in the air and on the surface. Notably, recent attacks have even directly encroached on Romania's territorial waters.
Given the complex developments, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte held separate talks with the leaders of Romania and Bulgaria to assess the level of threat to this vital shipping lane.
The Sofia (Bulgaria) authorities have submitted a detailed list of proposed technical assistance, including: fighter jets to reinforce the air force and air defense; ground-based air defense missile systems and electronic warfare equipment to neutralize UAVs; and long-range airborne surveillance radar systems to track low-flying targets.
On the Romanian side, the country continues to play an active role in proposing common security solutions for the Danube and Black Sea regions.
Currently, France has officially offered to provide technical assistance packages to the two Eastern European countries. Other major allies such as the US, Italy, Spain, Portugal , and Slovakia, which previously provided defensive equipment to Romania after the drone debris incidents in the Danube border region and the city of Galati, are also expected to soon announce further assistance plans.
In addition to supplementing reconnaissance equipment, NATO affirms it is tightening its defensive posture along its entire eastern flank, with a focus on enhancing anti-drone capabilities to protect maritime infrastructure and international trade security.

NATO will increase its military presence in the Black Sea, deploying additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems, and drones following a series of deadly attacks on commercial vessels in the region.
The announcement came after NATO's main decision-making body, the North Atlantic Council, met at the alliance's Brussels headquarters on Oct. 20 to discuss Black Sea security.
"Allies have or will send additional maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems, explosive exploitation teams, intelligence personnel, drones, and more to the Black Sea," U.S. Army Col. Martin O'Donnell, a NATO military spokesperson, said in a statement.
O'Donnell said NATO's immediate priority is improving its awareness of potential threats in the region through additional surveillance equipment and intelligence sharing.
The decision comes after a series of drone attacks on commercial vessels near the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria, raising concerns about the safety and security of shipping routes used by Ukraine and other countries in the region.
On Oct. 13, drones struck two commercial vessels off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast. The Maltese-flagged, Ukrainian-owned Chelsea 3 was hit by three drones near the coastal town of Byala, while the Guinea-Bissau-flagged HS Dignity sank near Krapets, leaving 11 crew members missing.
Bulgarian authorities subsequently recovered suspected drone fragments from the damaged Chelsea 3 and began the process of examining them to determine the weapon's origin, The Maritime Executive reported on Oct. 20.
Two days later, seven sailors were reported missing after the Wine Trader, a San Marino-flagged chemical tanker, caught fire near the Romanian port of Sulina amid reported drone activity.
NATO has not announced which country they think is responsible for the attacks. Military analysts have identified Russia as the likely perpetrator, although Moscow has not acknowledged responsibility.
"NATO has already strengthened our posture along the eastern flank, including with counter-drone capabilities," NATO spokesperson Allison Hart said on Oct. 20.
"We will continue to stand united and ensure that we are ready and able to address any threat and to keep our one billion people safe."
The attacks have prompted growing concerns among NATO members about the possibility of Russia's war against Ukraine spilling over into neighbouring countries.
On Oct. 17, Romanian F-16 fighter jets shot down two drones over the country's territorial waters, according to Romania's Defense Ministry.
Romanian Defense Minister Radu Miruta said the drones were believed to be Russian-made Geran-4 models, due to their speed and other characteristics.
The Black Sea is a critical route for Ukraine's agricultural exports, but attacks on commercial shipping have raised concerns about the risks faced by civilian crews and maritime security.
